title: MindOS — landing
text: MindOS: a memory and proof-of-work layer for AI agents Skip to content Autopilot v2 · source-available (FSL-1.1-MIT) · runs on your machine AI agents lose track of their work. MindOS is the memory they share. When you run several AI agents, each one only sees its own conversation. MindOS keeps one local record they all read and write: what was decided, what changed since, who is working on what, and what actually proves a job is finished. Everything stays in a single database file on your machine. Get started — 3 commands Read the architecture Python 3.9+ · no deps · SQLite home you own · no server to run 1 file you own and can read 5 states proof before done rehearse → undo one command an IdeatorX project · MindOS Agents, any brand anything that can run a command The rulebook one owner · proof before done · nothing silent Your local record one database file you own and can read every decision keeps its reason and replacement Move records in or out safely rehearses on a copy first · undoes with one command receipt sealed ✓ every claim ends with evidence A request moves from the CLI surface down through the guarantee checks into the SQLite authority and comes back sealed as a receipt. The problem How agent work falls apart, step by step. Nothing dramatic has to go wrong. A normal Tuesday is enough. Follow one task through an afternoon without a shared memory — then see how the same afternoon looks with one. An agent picks up the task It reads the goal into its own short-term context The session ends Everything it held in mind leaves with it A second agent takes over With no record of progress, it redoes the same work A decision changes upstream The old choice still looks current to everyone else “Done” gets claimed anyway Nobody can ask what proves it, because nothing does Five steps: task picked up, session ends, work repeated, decision goes stale, completion claimed without proof. Hover not needed — this rail reads top to bottom. Each dot is a moment where a shared record would have changed the outcome. None of this is a model problem. It is a memory problem. Chat transcripts, scratch files, and Git history each hold a fragment, but none of them can answer the simple questions: who is working on this right now, what changed while we were away, and what proves it is done? A day with MindOS One request, from words to finished work. Here is the same afternoon with MindOS present. It is not another chat window. It is the shared record every agent checks before acting and updates after acting. 1 You ask in plain words “Fix the render bug on the invoice page.” MindOS records the request as a task anyone can see, with a priority you set or that your lead agent sets. 2 An agent claims it, out loud Before starting, an agent registers that it owns this task and for how long. If it stops responding, everyone can see the claim expired instead of guessing. 3 Work leaves a trail as it happens The agent posts short notes while it works. If its session dies halfway through, the next agent reads those notes and continues instead of starting over. 4 Finished means proven When an agent says it is done, MindOS asks what proves it: test output, a health check, a file hash. The proof is stored as a receipt, and only then does the task close. 5 You get an honest answer Ask “what happened today?” and MindOS answers from the record: what was decided, what changed, what was completed and what stalled. Not from anyone’s recollection. Five moments, one line. The spine on the left is the same task — read top to bottom. What MindOS remembers The current decision, the old one, and why it changed. Notes in a file only hold the latest version. Git holds history but no meaning. MindOS keeps each decision with its validity window, so an agent can ask what was…

text: Documentation — MindOS Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Documentation Everything here is grounded in the runtime repository’s README, ARCHITECTURE, INSTALL, SECURITY, ROADMAP, CHANGELOG, and STABILITY docs. Each page links back to its source. MindOS is a local memory your agents share — one file that remembers what was decided, what changed, who owns what, and what proves a job is finished. It runs on your machine, needs no server or account, and every change keeps its reason and evidence. MindOS is the durable local operating system for Hermes and cooperating AI agents. Under that plain description it combines: one SQLite file as the execution authority ( execution truth — who did what and what proves it), a Hindsight shared semantic memory binding, temporal facts (decisions with validity windows), task ownership with time-boxed leases and fencing epochs, hash-sealed receipts, auditable provenance, plus session archives, profiles, skills, cron definitions, migration, recovery, and rollback — behind one CLI surface with no server to deploy. 01 Getting started Clone, init, doctor. Your first task in five commands. 02 Concepts Tasks, leases, fencing epochs, receipts, facts, handoffs. 03 Architecture CLI → guarantees → SQLite home → migration layer. 04 Installation Prerequisites, install, upgrading, health checks. 05 Migration Brain inventory, dry-run-first import, rollback. 06 Memory Hindsight binding, temporal facts, notes, recall packs. 07 Tasks and receipts Lifecycle, leases, evidence-linked completions. 08 Agents and handoffs Cross-agent protocol, acks, recall digests. 09 Recovery and rollback Stale-lease sweeps, resume, rollback journal. 10 Security Boundary contract, secret guard, data rules. 11 CLI reference autopilot.py and ops.py command surface. 12 FAQ Common questions, honest limitations. 13 Roadmap Shipped, next, and non-goals as of August 2026. title: Agents and handoffs
text: Agents and handoffs — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Agents and handoffs Source: README.md in the runtime repository · All docs The handoff protocol handoff transfers a task between agents with an objective and structured fields. The response embeds the full recall bundle — task header, dependencies, live handoff, receipts, and notes — so the receiving agent resumes with evidence rather than a chat summary. Resume: the recovery half resume is the one-call, idempotent recovery path for killed sessions: it reconstructs state and hands back the recall bundle without double-executing work. Lineage handoff-history walks the full sequence oldest → newest, showing how ownership, objective, and evidence evolved across agents. Secret guard note , supersede-note , and handoff scan their content with shape detectors (AWS keys, tokens, credential-shaped values) and block or redact by default. An explicit, itself-audited --allow-secret override exists for fleet sweeps that must locate them. ← Tasks and receipts Recovery and rollback → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Architecture
text: Architecture — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Architecture Source: ARCHITECTURE.md in the runtime repository · All docs In plain words: every request flows through a rulebook into one local database file you own, and verified answers flow back up. If a request would break the rules — stale owner, missing proof, leaked secret — it’s refused at the rulebook, before SQLite ever changes. MindOS answers one question continuously: what is true right now, and what evidence proves it? Every layer exists to keep SQLite the single execution authority ( execution truth — the record of who did what and what proves it) and to make every mutation auditable and reversible. CLI surface autopilot.py (tasks) · ops.py (fleet ops) · verify.py (suite) Rulebook one owner at a time · proof before done · secrets blocked · nothing silent · hash-chained history (fencing epochs, audit chain, receipt sealing, FTS search) Local record state.db — the single SQLite file you own (the authority) · temporal.db — optional sidecar for the evolving fact graph Move safely dry-run-first manifests · rollback journal · orphan quarantine · sealed brain inventory Core invariants Single authority — SQLite is the execution authority; Hindsight remains a shared semantic bank and is never copied into SQLite as a second one. Fail closed — ambiguity/corruption refuses with exact blockers; absent optional sources are recorded honestly without blocking. Evidence over claims — completions require sealed receipts; audit events are digest-only where values could be sensitive. Dry-run first — destructive operations plan first, apply only on an explicit flag, journal for rollback, and re-run idempotently. Source immutability — migration reads never mutate their sources; full-fixture hash comparisons prove it. The three surfaces autopilot.py handles the daily work — tasks, leases (time-boxed ownership with fencing epochs ), receipts (hash-sealed proof), facts (evolving decisions with reasons — temporal facts ), handoffs,…

title: Concepts
text: Concepts — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Concepts Source: README.md in the runtime repository · All docs In plain words: MindOS keeps one local file that answers three questions — who owns this right now, what changed while you were away, and what proves a job is done. The words below are just precise names for those ideas; each comes with a one-line plain meaning so the precise term never needs guessing. Tasks and ownership A task is the unit of work: project, title, priority, status, next action, dependency edges, and a full audited history. Work is claimed, not assigned — an agent says “I own this until X” and the record holds it. That claim is a live lease ; the fencing epoch is simply a number that ticks up each time the task changes hands, so an old worker can’t quietly overwrite a new one. Think “library checkout” — one borrower at a time, and the due stamp tells everyone else to wait. Leases and fencing epochs Every lease acquisition bumps lease_epoch . The holder passes that number back on every change, so a stale process is refused even when the owner name still matches. heartbeat proves the holder is still alive; renew extends the time without changing status; release hands a task back without burning retry budget. The epoch is the fencing that stops yesterday’s worker from acting as if it were still today’s owner. Sealed receipts A receipt is a small evidence file saved with tight permissions (0600) and a sha256 recorded in the audit trail. Completion requires one — “tests pass” typed in chat is not proof; only a stored, hash-sealed file counts. Temporal facts Facts are evolving statements — subject / predicate / object triples — each with a validity window and a reason for change ( provenance ). Use fact-assert to record one, facts to browse, and search-facts to search with BM25 retrieval and temporal rerank. Instead of overwriting, MindOS keeps “we used X, then X was replaced by Y because Y shipped faster” — so “what was true last Tuesday?” always has…

title: FAQ
text: FAQ — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 FAQ Source: README.md in the runtime repository · All docs Is MindOS open source? It is source-available under FSL-1.1-MIT — MIT-licensed after the applicable two-year change date. It is not OSI open source during the FSL restriction period. Is it a cloud service? No. There is no server to deploy. All state lives in a local SQLite home; MindOS never sends external messages or writes to external APIs. Does it replace Git? No. Git remains the right tool for code. MindOS is the operational layer Git was never designed to be — leases, receipts, recovery — and it complements rather than replaces your repos. What if Hindsight is down? The system degrades honestly: the binding is probed, absence is recorded as absent , and execution truth in SQLite continues uninterrupted. Hindsight is semantic memory, never a second authority. Honest limitations Leases prevent task collisions but seams (shared worktrees/branches) are refused at claim time, not merged safely. The secret guard is shape-based, not a general credential scanner. Packaging and single-command bootstrap are on the roadmap, not shipped. ← CLI reference Roadmap → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Getting started
text: Getting started — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Getting started Source: INSTALL.md in the runtime repository · All docs In plain words: MindOS is a local record on your machine — no server to deploy, no account to create, no third-party packages to install. Pick a folder, run three commands, and you have a shared memory your agents can all read and write. MindOS is a local record on your machine — there is no server to deploy and no third-party packages. Some docs call this a control plane , which just means one place that decides and remembers. Python 3.9+ on macOS or Linux is the only prerequisite. git clone <repo-url> mindos cd mindos export MINDOS_HOME ="$HOME/.hermes/mindos" # any writable path works python3 autopilot.py init python3 ops.py doctor # health-check the new home init creates the SQLite schema ( state.db , plus temporal.db when the fact graph is used). All commands accept the home via MINDOS_HOME / HERMES_AUTOPILOT_HOME . Your first task python3 autopilot.py create --project Trove --title "Ship render fix" --priority P1 python3 autopilot.py claim tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --minutes 30 python3 autopilot.py heartbeat tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --note "Running verification" python3 autopilot.py receipt tsk_4f2a --kind verification --payload '{"tests":"pass"}' python3 autopilot.py complete tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --note "tests pass" Completions require a live lease and a sealed receipt — claims without evidence are rejected by policy, not by convention. Seeding an initial queue (optional) seed_current_state.py demonstrates upserting a task queue without executing any work. Point it at your own home and edit the item list first. title: Memory
text: Memory — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Memory Source: ARCHITECTURE.md in the runtime repository · All docs In plain words: MindOS remembers decisions the way you’d want — the current answer, the old answer it replaced, and why it changed — plus notes that never silently overwrite each other. An agent can ask “what was true last Tuesday?” and get a real answer with its reason. Hindsight binding Hindsight is the shared semantic memory — the place where meaning is looked up — accessed through an explicit, provider-neutral binding. SQLite stays the single execution authority (the local file that decides what counts as done); Hindsight is never copied into it as a second one. When Hindsight is unreachable, the system degrades honestly: affected sources are recorded as absent rather than guessed at. Temporal facts python3 autopilot.py fact-assert --subject service-auth --predicate uses --object postgres-14 --source codex python3 autopilot.py facts --subject service-auth python3 autopilot.py search-facts postgres --rank Temporal facts are evolving statements — subject / predicate / object — each with a validity window , provenance (where it came from and why), and supersession (what it replaced). Ownership, priorities, and decisions stay queryable over time, with BM25 retrieval and temporal hybrid rerank. “We used cache A, then replaced it with cache B because B shipped faster” — both stay readable, with the reason attached. Notes with supersession Notes supersede rather than overwrite: the history of what was believed, when, and by whom is preserved and audited. All free-text fields pass the secret guard (credential-shaped values are blocked or redacted before storage). ← Migration Tasks and receipts → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Migration
text: Migration — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Migration Source: INSTALL.md in the runtime repository · All docs Migration moves non-execution brain surfaces (memory archives, sessions, profiles, skills, cron definitions) across without turning Hindsight into a second authority, and imports execution truth into a fresh home. Sealed brain inventory python3 ops.py brain-inventory --out inventory.json python3 ops.py brain-inventory-check inventory.json # verify the seal Nine source kinds are covered — Autopilot, Hindsight binding, temporal sidecar, Claude memory sync, memory archives, sessions, profiles/skills, cron definitions — read-only, redacted, with sealed manifests. Hindsight is probed with GETs only; the shared bank is never written. Dry-run-first import python3 ops.py migrate-import … --dry-run # plan against a disposable target python3 ops.py migrate-import … # apply; journal written for rollback python3 ops.py migrate-rollback … # one-command recovery Foreign receipts are quarantined with full provenance instead of breaking foreign-key integrity. Re-runs are idempotent; source immutability is proven by full-fixture hash comparisons in the end-to-end suite. ← Installation Memory → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Recovery and rollback
text: Recovery and rollback — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Recovery and rollback Source: ARCHITECTURE.md in the runtime repository · All docs Guarded stale-lease recovery recover sweeps stale leases with guarded, reported skips so mid-sweep claims are never wiped. leases --all previews exactly what a sweep would take. Killed sessions resume gives idempotent killed-session recovery with the full recall bundle — no double execution, no lost evidence. Migration rollback python3 ops.py migrate-import … --dry-run # plan first python3 ops.py migrate-import … # journal written python3 ops.py migrate-rollback … # target restored to pre-import state Everything destructive plans first: dry-run manifests, explicit apply flag, rollback journal, idempotent re-runs. Orphans are quarantined with provenance, never dropped. Integrity verify-chain recomputes the audit hash chain and reports tampering, with checkpoint-based truncation detection. ops.py doctor adds FTS5 drift detection via fts5vocab . ← Agents and handoffs Security → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Roadmap
text: Roadmap — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Roadmap Source: ROADMAP.md in the runtime repository · All docs Honest status as of August 2026. Nothing is claimed as done unless it ships in the runtime repository with verify coverage. Shipped (v1) Task registry with live leases, fencing epochs, retry budgets, backoff, dependency edges, impact analysis, dispatch planning, and metrics. Hash-chained audit stream with tamper detection ( verify-chain ). Sealed receipts and approval receipts (0600 files + sha256). Notes with supersession; provenance-linked temporal fact graph. Cross-agent handoffs with recall digests; session retention ( sessions-prune ). Secret guard (block/redact/audited override) over all free-text fields. Doctor health checks incl. FTS5 drift detection via fts5vocab. Dry-run-first migration layer: inventory, import, orphan-receipt quarantine, rollback journal, idempotent re-runs, source immutability proofs. End-to-end brain inventory across nine source kinds with sealed manifests. Next Hourly control tower — report task changes on a schedule without executing work. Cross-agent probe hardening — broader post-install recall/handoff probes. Policy expansion — more project policies gating automatic side effects per client. Parallel MindOS home — verified parallel installation with one-command rollback. Packaging — single-command bootstrap and versioned release notes. Non-goals Cloud hosting, external messaging, code deployment, or becoming a second semantic-memory authority alongside Hindsight. ← FAQ Docs index → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Security
text: Security — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Security Source: SECURITY.md in the runtime repository · All docs What MindOS will never do (v1 contract) MindOS is a registry and evidence layer. It does not: deploy, merge, or push code; send external messages or call external APIs for writes; submit applications or take side effects on any external system; run arbitrary agent commands; or access Keychain values or credential stores. Data boundary All state lives in a local SQLite home ( $MINDOS_HOME ). The repository itself must never contain live databases, receipts, installation reports, session archives, Hindsight exports, backups, runtime artifacts, .env files, or Claude memory contents. Secret guard Every user-supplied text field passes shape detectors that block, redact, or — only under an explicit, audited override — allow credential-shaped values, so fleet sweeps can still locate them. Legacy rows sitting in live notes/handoffs are reported with the same detectors. Tamper-evident audit A global hash-chained event stream records every transition; verify-chain recomputes the chain and reports tampering. Audit events are digest-only where values could be sensitive. ← Recovery and rollback CLI reference → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close

title: Tasks and receipts
text: Tasks and receipts — MindOS docs Skip to content Documentation Getting started Concepts Architecture Installation Migration Memory Tasks and receipts Agents and handoffs Recovery and rollback Security CLI reference FAQ Roadmap MindOS — Autopilot v2 Tasks and receipts Source: README.md in the runtime repository · All docs In plain words: a task is a to-do that can only have one owner at a time, needs a heartbeat to stay alive, and can’t be called done until a proof file is sealed. Every step is written down. Lifecycle Tasks move through claim → heartbeat → receipt → complete (or fail ). Every transition is audited. next --claim dispatches by priority, deadline class, aging fairness, and optional critical-path tie-breaking ( --prefer-unblocking ). Leases in practice python3 autopilot.py claim tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --minutes 30 # → lease_epoch: 1 python3 autopilot.py heartbeat tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --epoch 1 python3 autopilot.py renew tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --minutes 45 python3 autopilot.py complete tsk_4f2a --owner hermes --epoch 1 --note "tests pass" A mismatch fails with lease superseded (held epoch N, current M); reclaim … . leases gives a fleet-wide live view; --all includes expired-but-still-held leases (recovery candidates). Receipts Receipts are hash-sealed evidence files (0600 + sha256 in the audit trail). Completion policy requires one, so "done" always carries proof. Failures feed retry budgets and dispatch backoff instead of disappearing. Dependencies, impact, critical path blocked-by asks what holds a task; impact walks the DAG downward; critical-path reports the longest unfinished chain — the minimum number of sequential dispatch waves needed to drain the open graph. ← Memory Agents and handoffs → ↑ ↓ navigate ↵ open esc close
